prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network always picks DONE at once, so it scores 0. The likely reason is the mirror rule. An action at column x places its brick at column 8-dx-x, but the convolutional placement head only sees features near the anchor cell. The cells that matter are on the mirrored side of the board, which can be up to 7 columns away and outside a 5-cell receptive field. So the network cannot tell which placements are good. Random placements mostly earn negative reward, PPO learns that DONE (reward 0) is the safest choice, and it stops exploring.

The fix is to let each anchor see features from its landing cells. If the feature map is flipped left-right, a brick's footprint at anchor x lines up exactly with the cells it actually fills, so ordinary footprint pooling works. These first trials test that fix in two ways: a fixed flip, and a learned mixing layer across columns. A third trial pairs the flip with a recipe change that gives more updates and more entropy, to fight the early DONE collapse.

### Round 2
Mirroring the features before the placement head is what makes learning work: r1c1 reached 0.53 while the starting network scored 0.00. Changing only the recipe in r1c2 (more, smaller updates and entropy 0.02) raised this to 0.90. That gain is much larger than the gap between seeds. Letting the network learn the column mapping instead (r1c3) failed (0.02), so the fixed flip should stay. In r1c2, training success was still rising at the end (0.84 at 75% of training, 0.90 at 100%), so more samples or more updates should help. Dev mean IoU is 0.99 with few wrong cells, so the remaining failures are probably occasional wrong placements or wrong order around overhangs. This round tests three things against r1c2: 2 PPO epochs (about 227k steps instead of 158k), a summary of the whole board added to the placement head, and a deeper trunk with a wider view, also trained with 2 epochs, to compare against the first.

### Round 3
The mirror-aware head was the key fix. Flipping the trunk features before the footprint-pooling head took dev success from 0 to 0.53 (r1c1). A learned column mixer did not learn the mapping within the budget (0.02). After that, the recipe mattered most. Using 128 environments with 3 epochs and entropy 0.02 gave 0.90 (r1c2), and dropping to 2 epochs, which buys more fresh samples, gave 0.919 (r2c1, seeds 0.92/0.91). In both runs training success was still rising at the end, so the run is short of samples rather than capacity. Adding global context to the head (0.875) was within noise, so it did not help. A deeper dilated trunk hurt and was unstable across seeds (0.82/0.33). Failed builds have IoU of about 0.99, so the errors are small near misses. This round makes three single recipe changes to the best trial: 1 PPO epoch for more samples, a higher discount so the exact-build bonus reaches earlier steps, and smaller batches for more updates.

### Round 4
Joining the trunk features with their left-right flip is what made the task learnable (0 to about 0.9). On the recipe side, 128 envs and 2 PPO epochs give the best result (r2c1, 0.919). Recipes that push for more, smaller updates (1 epoch; 64 envs) collapsed to pressing DONE straight away, scoring 0 on both seeds. Collapse to DONE is the main risk. A deeper trunk and global context in the head did not help. Gamma 0.99 gave the best single seed (0.953) but its two seeds were far apart (0.95 and 0.79). This last round keeps r2c1's sample budget and tries to make training less likely to collapse: orthogonal initialisation that starts the policy close to uniform, higher entropy, and gamma 0.99 with that initialisation. These are low-risk changes aimed at beating 0.919.

## Trial it ended with
name: mirror + 2 PPO epochs
hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r1c2, but with ppo_epochs set to 2. The budget then allows about 227k steps (about 110 updates) instead of about 158k. r1c2's training success was still rising when training stopped, so more fresh designs should help more than reusing each sample a third time. Refuted if dev success falls below 0.86, meaning the third epoch mattered more than the extra samples.

naming the round it comes from).
